title: Historian uncovers 'oldest' photographic evidence of poltergeist
excerpt: A historian has uncovered photographs hidden in a 1905 magazine that capture the damage caused during a notorious haunting that turned a Lancashire village into a national sensation
content:
Lost photos of terrifying poltergeist that wrecked family home discovered

A historian has uncovered photographs hidden in a 1905 magazine that capture the damage caused during a notorious haunting that turned a Lancashire village into a national sensation

19:47, 15 Oct 2026

For weeks during the summer of 1904, a family lived in fear and terror as pieces of heavy stone, mortar and plaster were reportedly hurled across their home in the dead of night. A first floor bedroom was the centre of unexplained chaos, and the mystery was widely attributed to a poltergeist.

‌

‌

As news of the disorder spread, the strange occurrence drew crowds of people, including reporters, investigators, and spiritualists from across the country, who gathered in the churchyard opposite the house, in Up Holland, West Lancashire, hoping to catch a glimpse of the unexplained disturbances and uncover the truth.

‌

Now, more than 120 years later, historian Stephen Miller believes he has uncovered the world’s oldest known photographic evidence of poltergeist activity, images that had been largely forgotten since their publication in Wide World Magazine in 1905.

‌

Damaged bedroom windows and piles of rubble

The photographs show a damaged, blocked-up bedroom window and a pile of rubble scattered across the floor, offering a rare visual record of one of Lancashire’s most intriguing paranormal mysteries.

Stephen, 42, who grew up near Blackburn and now lives in West Yorkshire, discovered the images while researching the case for his podcast, The Poltergeist Project.

‌

He told the ECHO: “I've always had a kind of interest in all things a bit weird and wonderful. As a sceptic, more than kind of a believer trying to prove anything.

“I was looking round, trawling through old newspapers, and I came across the Up Holland story and thought that’s weird enough that I can’t just explain it easily without doing a bit more digging.

‌

“Outside of the village, it seemed like not a lot had been done about it, so I thought that would be a good one for me to start digging into.”

The disturbances began with knocks, bangs and strange tapping noises inside the home of widow Alice Winstanley, who had seven children, three girls and four boys. Her eldest daughter had moved out of the family home on Church Street, leaving Alice living with her remaining siblings.

‌

The house sat right next door to the White Lion pub and opposite St Thomas the Martyr Parish Church.

But the situation became increasingly alarming when sections of an old, blocked-up window in her son’s bedroom began to break apart, with pieces of masonry apparently flying across the room and into other parts of the house.

The family were left 'terrified'

One night, Alice’s sons reportedly witnessed the material flying around their bedroom and were left terrified.

‌

Alice turned to the police for help before approaching local councillors including Cllr Baxter and Cllr Bibby, who became involved in investigating the strange occurrences.

Despite attempts to keep the matter quiet, news spread rapidly through the small village.

‌

For much of August 1904, hundreds and reportedly thousands of people gathered in the churchyard opposite the house, peering through its windows in the hope of witnessing something extraordinary.

Stephen said the crowds became increasingly rowdy, with some treating the spectacle as an evening’s entertainment, while psychic investigators sought access to the property.

He said: “It was a small place and it was making quite a lot of noise and gossip. It became a bit of a circus, really, and obviously a bit distressing for the family.”

‌

But the household was a far cry from the sensational image of a haunted house that developed around it. Alice was a 49-year-old widow whose husband had died a couple of years earlier.

Her sons, who followed in their father’s footsteps and worked in the coal mines, shared a small bedroom, while the family’s younger daughters and their mother slept in another room.

‌

Stephen said: “They were a very normal working-class family. The dad had been a coal miner and the boys had all gone into the pits. The girls grew up, became weavers, and worked with cotton.

“They were a very typical Lancashire working-class family of the time. Nothing weird or wacky about them. It just occurred to them, unfortunately for them.”

The alleged activity took a heavy emotional toll on the household, with Alice reportedly turning to prayer and religious visitors in the hope of bringing the disturbances to an end.

‌

Stephen said: “They were genuinely scared and just wanted it to go away.”

The explanations

As the story spread beyond Up Holland, competing explanations emerged. Sceptics suggested the boys might have been responsible, while others pointed to possible structural subsidence or vibrations from passing tractors.

‌

But Stephen said he struggled to find a convincing explanation for the accounts of masonry apparently being thrown across the room.

He said: “The number one is that the boys were doing it, and as a sceptic, that’s probably the most likely situation.

“But then a lot of the witnesses describe it as not being possible that they did it. They were sat in the room with them whilst it was happening, and the boys were safely tucked up asleep in bed, and these things were still flying around.

‌

“So there is quite a lot of evidence against them doing it.”

Those who believed the house was haunted had their own theory: that the disturbances were being caused by the spirit of George Lyon, a notorious local highwayman who was hanged in Lancaster in 1815.

Lyon was buried just metres from the house, in the churchyard of St Thomas, prompting rumours that his ghost had returned in search of treasure supposedly hidden inside the property’s walls.

‌

Stephen said: “I am at present unable to explain the things that were happening.

“Although I’m a sceptic, I’m not a huge believer in the paranormal, I try to have an open mind and, if I can’t explain it rationally, that doesn’t mean I’m going to say it was the Up Holland highwayman.

“It just means I can’t explain it.”

‌

The discovery of the photographs

It was while attempting to piece together the original evidence that Stephen stumbled upon the photographs. He had found references to pictures taken during the investigation but could not locate the images themselves.

A report led him to Wide World Magazine, prompting him to track down a copy of the 1905 publication.

‌

Inside, he found photographs of two councillors involved in the investigation, alongside the images of the damaged window and rubble.

Stephen said: “I’d never seen any evidence from that early to do with the poltergeist case, so it was fantastic to find evidence.

“I was mostly excited because in my imagination from reading the accounts, it was like little bits of stone and plaster. It's hard to imagine exactly what it was, and in the photograph, you can see just how much damage was caused and how much material had been pulled from the wall.”

‌

The discovery prompted him to question whether the photographs might be the earliest of their kind.

He compared them with images associated with other famous paranormal cases, including Borley Rectory in the 1930s and the Enfield poltergeist investigation in the 1970s.

‌

After searching for earlier examples and asking contacts in the field, Stephen was unable to find any photographs that predated the Up Holland images.

He believes their significance has been overlooked partly because the magazine containing them gradually disappeared from view, while previous accounts of the case tended to treat it as an unusual piece of local history.

He said: “The more I dug, the more I started to get excited that actually, I think this is the earliest photograph in the world of evidence of poltergeist activity.

“I've been challenging and asking people and no one's provided any earlier, and I just can't imagine there being any.”

The house itself was eventually demolished in 1934 to make way for road widening, but Stephen hopes the discovery of the photographs will bring renewed attention to the national mystery.
